newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: World Bank critical of Uzbekistan forex controls.
newsitem.headline: World Bank critical of Uzbekistan forex controls.

text.p: A senior World Bank official on Tuesday criticised Uzbekistan's foreign exchange controls as the spread between the official and black market rates for the Uzbek sum continued to widen.

"It is hard to understand why the Uzbekistan government should now introduce foreign exchange and additional foreign trade controls and in fact move backwards from its stated objective of introducing current account convertibility of the sum," Hasso Molineus, resident representative of the World Bank in Uzbekistan told Reuters in an interview.

On Tuesday, the black market rate for the sum traded in a range of 125-130 to the dollar as opposed to the official rate set by the national bank of 51.10. Up until the end of August, the black market rate had hovered around 25-30 percent above the official rate.
Molineus said: "The increasing spread between the official and the black market rate of the sum reflects an uncertainty in the investment community with regard to the impact of these controls."

There was no immediate official response to Molineus' remarks. But his comments come at an awkward time for Uzbekistan, where a mission from the International Monetary Fund is just about to wind up a visit.
In the last few weeks, many shops have had to shut because of a shortage of foreign exchange.

One Western businessman selling consumer goods in this desert nation of 23 million complained that exchange controls meant 'suitcase traders' from neighbouring former Soviet republics were able to snap up his goods and sell them at a profit for below his own asking price.
Uzbek President Islam Karimov, the former communist party boss, has said he would prefer to see foreign exchange spent on importing new technologies rather than on "foreign chewing gum".
Observers say the controls signal a shortage of hard currency. Karimov has also started a high-profile building programme to modernise Tashkent and other Uzbek cities.

But an official at Uzbekistan's national bank for foreign economic activity said: "Since October, all firms, resident and non-resident, have faced difficulties with converting the currency. The central bank has cut almost twice the volume of convertible currency."
In 1994, the government said it would introduce full convertibility of the sum by the beginning of 1997.
In 1995, the volume of trade in dollars totalled 1.5 billion.
According to the official press, an earlier estimate for the volume of trade in foreign currency of $3 billion for this year was recently revised down to just over $2 billion.
In October, the Uzbek government cut the number of banks allowed to trade foreign currency from 14 to two, saying there had been mismanagement in hard currency dealings.

Molineus dismissed rumours that Uzbekistan, the world's ninth largest gold producer, has nearly exhausted its foreign exchange reserves. "Uzbekistan is one of the few CIS countries which was quite successful in its macroeconomic stabilisation programme," he said.
"For example, the budget deficit is under four percent, inflation is manageable and foreign currency reserves are quite adequate," Molineus said.

He said while the World Bank was concerned at "unfortunate developments", he said it would continue with its assistance programmes, "as long as our investments are not negatively affected by the Uzbek government."
The World Bank currently supports programmes in water supply, health and cotton production.
